sentences.text: Preondactylus was approximately the size of a modern pigeon.
This small pterosaur possessed short wings with a total wingspan of only 45 centimeters and relatively long legs.
Its mouth contained single-cusp teeth, each featuring a single sharp point.
The widely spaced, pointed teeth did not touch one another, resulting in an absence of tooth wear.
Although Preondactylus had short wings considered a primitive feature, it was a fully developed flier.
Evidence suggests the second specimen was preserved inside the gastric pellet of a predatory fish that vomited it up after eating the pterosaur.

The original fossil slab containing the first specimen was accidentally broken into pieces during extraction, forcing researchers to study it using a silicone rubber cast made from a negative imprint on stone.
Preondactylus lived approximately 217 to 214 million years ago in what is now Italy.
The species Preondactylus buffarinii was discovered by Nando Buffarini in 1982 in the Preone valley of the Italian Alps.
A second specimen, MFSN-1891, was found in 1984 approximately 150 to 200 meters deeper in the strata than the original discovery.
A third specimen, MFSN 25161, consists of a partial skull that lacks the lower jaws.
Preondactylus was described and named by Rupert Wild in 1984.
Rupert Wild initially classified Preondactylus within Rhamphorhynchidae, but it was later understood to be much more basal.
David Unwin identified Preondactylus as the most basal pterosaur and used it to define the node for the clade Pterosauria.

Some phylogenetic analyses have placed Preondactylus in a somewhat more derived position than the most basal, while other analyses have considered a somewhat more advanced position for Preondactylus within the suborder Pterodactylia.
